title: SDK flush heuristics across popular HTTP/gRPC clients — lab notes
content:
Summary:
This lab investigates how client-side "flush" semantics in common SDKs and HTTP clients affect end-to-end streaming latency and server-side batching behavior. The aim is to understand microburst creation, interaction with the server's batching and KV-cache warmup, and how flush differences change tail percentiles for short-lived streams (inference-first-token to final-token times).

Motivation / problem statement:
We frequently see 50–200ms variability in first-byte and tail latency for streaming requests even when server CPU/GPU utilization is steady. Hypothesis: client libraries emit application writes with different buffering/flush behavior (syscall frequency, TLS record boundary alignment, HTTP/2 frame boundaries) which causes the server to receive bursts or sparse token inputs that interact poorly with continuous batching and proxy buffering. This becomes visible in low-latency workloads (<= 200ms target).

Test matrix (what we ran):
- Clients: Go net/http (http2 via golang.org/x/net/http2), curl 7.80+ (HTTP/2), okhttp3 (Java, http/2 via OkHttp), node-fetch (node 16 http2 client), python aiohttp (httpx + h2), grpc-go (streaming), grpc-java (streaming).
- Transports: HTTP/2 over TLS, gRPC over HTTP/2 (TLS), and one control run HTTP/1.1 for coarse comparison.
- Payloads: small interactive prompts (avg 80B request, expected 3–8 token responses), and mid-length prompts (1–2KB request, 20–60 token responses).
- Server: local dev-serving runtime with batching disabled vs. batching enabled (window=20ms, max-batch=16), edge proxy present vs. bypassed.
- Metrics captured: time-to-first-byte (TTFB), time-to-final-token, per-token inter-arrival on server, TLS-record sizes, syscall write frequency on client, HTTP/2 frame boundaries, server batch latency and batch size distribution.
- Runs: 10k requests per client type, randomized ordering, collected p50/p90/p99 numbers.

Key observations (high level):
1) Flush frequency correlates strongly with server-side microburst formation. Clients that perform frequent small syscalls (e.g., Python sync clients, naive Node implementations) produce a high number of small TLS records, which the edge/proxy tends to coalesce unpredictably — causing both extra queuing and uneven batching behavior on the server.
2) OkHttp and Go http2 implementations coalesce application writes into larger TLS records more consistently; these clients yielded fewer but larger batches on server, reducing p99 by ~15–25ms in our low-latency config.
3) grpc implementations (grpc-go, grpc-java) expose streaming primitives that tend to flush per-message; depending on message sizes, that produced either good streaming interactivity (for medium-sized message boundaries) or very chatty behavior when the application emitted many tiny messages.
4) Edge proxy buffering has a non-linear impact: when proxy buffering is enabled, many small records are coalesced into a single egress flush which can reduce syscall overhead but increases server-side burstiness and worsens variance for requests that rely on early partial outputs.
5) TLS record boundaries matter: when client flushes align with semantic token boundaries, server can stream partial tokens earlier. Misaligned flushes can add 10–40ms tail latency due to record coalescing and proxy-induced buffering windows.

Representative numbers (short prompts, batching enabled, with proxy):
- Go net/http: p50 42ms, p90 68ms, p99 112ms
- OkHttp: p50 40ms, p90 62ms, p99 98ms
- node-fetch naive: p50 52ms, p90 91ms, p99 160ms
- python requests (sync): p50 59ms, p90 110ms, p99 210ms
- grpc-go streaming (default): p50 45ms, p90 70ms, p99 130ms
Notes: numbers are medians from the run; absolute values depend on infra but relative deltas repeatable.

Detailed findings / diagnostics:
- Syscall traces: using bpftrace on client nodes showed that node and python had an order of magnitude higher write() syscall count per request versus Go and OkHttp. Higher syscall count correlates with smaller average TLS record size (often < 300B).
- TLS analysis: captured record sizes with tcpdump+ssldump shows Python/node records often cut inside UTF-8 tokens, creating framing that proxies may treat as flush points. This leads to proxy egress timers batching multiple small app records into one network packet — delaying the server's receipt of the first token until proxy flush.
- HTTP/2 frames: Go and OkHttp tend to pack multiple DATA frames into the same TLS record when the app writes happen quickly; h2 libraries that flush per write create more HTTP/2 DATA frames with smaller sizes.
- Server-side inter-arrival / batching: the runtime's batching window frequently saw either many single-request tiny batches (when clients were chatty) or larger batches (when clients coalesced) — both have tradeoffs. Chatty clients increase scheduling overhead; overly-coalesced clients increase first-token latency for interactive responses.

Root causes (synthesis):
- Client SDKs differ in buffering strategy (OS socket buffer usage, language runtime buffering, HTTP/2 libraries explicitly coalescing or not).
- Edge proxies introduce a buffering/coalescing layer and have different timers that interact with small-record arrival patterns.
- gRPC semantics (per-message flush) encourage libraries to flush at message boundaries; when apps send many small semantic messages this becomes chatty.

Short-term mitigations (what we can do in the next sprint):
1) SDK recommendations: Add a "flush mode" option in official SDKs: default coalesce (small jitter before flush when latency target > X ms), interactive mode (flush aggressively but with rate limiting to avoid microburst). Document recommended settings per latency SLO.
2) Server-side: adapt batching to detect chatty clients by measuring per-request per-token inter-arrival variance; if variance high, switch to a slightly longer aggregation window (e.g., +5–10ms) for that connection to smooth scheduling.
3) Proxy tuning: short-term change: adjust proxy egress timer to a smaller value for HTTP/2 streams marked as low-latency (if applicable), or bypass proxy coalescing for certain routes.

Longer-term changes / product notes:
- Expose an SDK-level API that allows calling applications to annotate writes with "semantic boundary" vs "can-coalesce" which our client libraries translate into coalesce heuristics. This helps apps that intentionally emit many small messages (e.g., token-by-token UIs).
- Work with language maintainers (e.g., okhttp/h2) to publish recommended flush/coalescing patches; consider shipping preconfigured wrappers in Redwood SDKs that apply these adjustments out-of-the-box.
- Add telemetry to the console that surfaces per-connection write patterns (avg write size, TLS-record size distribution) so customers can triage flaky latency.

Experimental notes (what didn't work):
- Adding random jitter to client-side flush had mixed results: it smoothed some p99 but increased p50 slightly for many clients; jitter is brittle to prompt distributions and user expectations.
- Forcing server to always use longer batching window hurt throughput at high QPS and increased GPU latency percentiles.

Action items (owners and rough timeline):
- Build a minimal "coalescing wrapper" in node+python SDKs and ship as opt-in by end of sprint: owner Ravi (2 weeks).
- Add connection-level write telemetry to runtime (small feature flag): owner Jia (3 weeks).
- Run a controlled A/B with proxy egress timer tuned for low-latency routes in staging: owner Liam (1 week to set up, 2 weeks to collect data).
- Draft SDK guidance doc and quickstart examples for interactive vs throughput workloads: owner Asha (this doc => finalize in 1 week).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How often do customer applications do token-by-token flushes intentionally? Survey CS for apps that might break on coalescing.
- Is there a reliable heuristics signal we can use server-side to avoid penalizing well-behaved chatty apps? (e.g., explicit header, or handshake bit)

Appendix: short checklist for reproducing locally
- Run the streaming-probes harness (github linked). Use --client {go,okhttp,node,python,grpc} --prompt-size small --qps 10 --duration 30m.
- Capture pcap and bpftrace traces; check tls record size distribution: pcap -> tlsrecords.csv and plot.
- Toggle proxy on/off to see delta.

Notes to self: keep this doc as the canonical lab notes; follow up with a concise one-pager for SDK owners and a separate internal RFC describing the new "flush mode" API."
